explanations.explanation: Slave is the word. The writer says, "The princess of the provinces has become a slave." Look at the drop in that one line, friend. Princess to slave is a long way down, and the writer just says it plainly.

A queen would be a step UP, and this verse only goes down. The writer says, "The princess of the provinces has become a slave." Same woman, opposite direction. Nobody in this verse is getting a crown.
No wedding bells in this verse, friend. The line just before it says she "…has become a widow." and then the princess has become a slave. The word you want is slave.
Her enemies. The writer says, "All her friends have betrayed her; they have become her enemies." That's a different kind of hurt than a stranger turning on you. These were the ones she counted on.

Servants would mean they were on her side, friend. The text goes the other way: "All her friends have betrayed her; they have become her enemies." Betraying someone is the opposite of being on their side.
Nobody's coming over for cookies in this verse. The writer says the friends "…have become her enemies." Guests show up to be with you, and these friends betrayed her.

I wish that were true, friend, but the verse says otherwise. "Among all her lovers there is no one to comfort her." Not one of them shows up. So the answer is False, and I think that's the loneliest part of the whole verse. (Lamentations 1:2)

False, and the text is blunt about it. "Among all her lovers there is no one to comfort her." She weeps aloud in the night, with tears upon her cheeks. The verse adds that all her friends have betrayed her and become her enemies, so nobody is coming. (Lamentations 1:2)

No place to rest. The writer says Judah "…dwells among the nations but finds no place to rest." She's living somewhere, but she can't settle. I know that feeling of being somewhere without being home.

No road home shows up in this verse. The writer says she "…dwells among the nations but finds no place to rest." Even her pursuers have "…overtaken her in the midst of her distress." The road is the one thing this verse leaves out.

A warm welcome would've been nice, friend, but the verse doesn't give her one. She "…dwells among the nations but finds no place to rest." Living among people and being welcomed by them are two different things. The verse says she finds no place to rest, and that's the answer.

Her many transgressions. The writer says, "For the LORD has brought her grief because of her many transgressions." The text gives the reason right there, so we don't have to guess. This is the poem being honest about the cause, and that honesty comes back later in the poem.
The army isn't the reason the writer gives. The verse says, "For the LORD has brought her grief because of her many transgressions." The writer points to transgressions, not to soldiers.
Nothing about harvests in this verse, friend. The writer says the LORD brought her grief "…because of her many transgressions." The reason is in the text, and it isn't the crops.
Too weak to flee. The writer says her princes "…lack the strength to flee in the face of the hunter." Deer with no pasture have nothing left in the tank. They can't even run.
I'd love to see that, but it's the opposite. The writer says they "…lack the strength to flee in the face of the hunter." A deer with no pasture has nothing left to run on.

No stand-off in this verse, friend. The princes are like deer that "…find no pasture…" and they "…lack the strength to flee in the face of the hunter." The verse says they can't flee, and that's the answer.

Looking away in shame would have been a mercy, and the verse doesn't give it. It says, "Her enemies looked upon her, laughing at her downfall." They looked, and they laughed. I think this is one of the lonelier lines in the poem.
False. The writer says, "Her enemies looked upon her, laughing at her downfall." They didn't look away, they looked and laughed. That's a heavy line, and the poem doesn't soften it.
That's the part that's off, friend. The writer says, "she did not consider her end." The verse never says she saw her downfall coming a long way off. So this one is False.

False. The writer says, "she did not consider her end." and calls her downfall "astounding." Nothing in the verse says she saw it coming from a long way off. And the verse says there was "…no one to comfort her."

The LORD. The poem cries, "Look, O LORD, on my affliction, for the enemy has triumphed!" When nobody else is there to comfort her, the cry goes up to Him. I think that's a strong thing to do in the middle of all this.
The princes are already in trouble, friend. The poem says they're like deer that "…lack the strength to flee…" The cry for someone to look goes elsewhere: "Look, O LORD, on my affliction…"
The priests are busy groaning in this poem. Verse 4 says, "her priests groan…" The one asked to look is the LORD: "Look, O LORD, on my affliction, for the enemy has triumphed!"

Forbidden. The poem says she has seen the nations enter her sanctuary, "…those You had forbidden to enter Your assembly." God had forbidden it, and she saw them enter her sanctuary. That's the heartbreak in this line.
No invitations went out, friend. The text says these were the nations "…You had forbidden to enter Your assembly." Forbidden and invited are opposites, and the verse picks forbidden.
Allowed would make this a much smaller heartbreak. The poem says these were the ones "…You had forbidden to enter Your assembly." The word in the verse is forbidden.

True. The text says, "They have traded their treasures for food to keep themselves alive." Verse 11 also says all her people "…groan as they search for bread." Treasures traded for food, just to stay alive.

It's true, and that's what makes it hard to read. The text says, "They have traded their treasures for food to keep themselves alive." Her people are groaning as they search for bread. Treasures that mattered once are now being swapped just to get by.

If any sorrow compares. The poem asks, "Is there any sorrow like mine, which was inflicted on me, which the LORD made me suffer on the day of His fierce anger?" It's a cry to everyone passing by to stop and look. I think it's the sound of someone who needs to be seen.
Walls aren't what the question is about, friend. The poem says, "Look around and see! Is there any sorrow like mine…" It's asking about sorrow, not stonework.
I get why you'd guess it, because friends are missing all over this poem. But here the question to the passersby is, "Is there any sorrow like mine…" The speaker wants them to see the sorrow.
True. The poem asks about the sorrow "…which the LORD made me suffer on the day of His fierce anger?" The poem says it plainly and doesn't dodge. It's a heavy line, so we'll let it sit for a moment.
It's true, friend, and the poem doesn't hide it. The sorrow is described as the one "…which the LORD made me suffer on the day of His fierce anger?" Heavy words, and they're right there in the verse.

Safe passage sounds nice, but that's not what this net does. The poem says, "He spread a net for my feet and turned me back." A net like that stops you in your tracks. Nobody's getting carried anywhere.
False. The poem says, "He spread a net for my feet and turned me back." This net catches feet and turns the speaker around. It's a picture of being stopped, not carried.
Neck. The poem says the transgressions "…are draped over my neck…" That's what a yoke does, friend. It sits on the neck and makes every step heavier.
Feet belong to the net, and you're thinking of verse 13: "He spread a net for my feet…" The yoke goes somewhere else. The transgressions "…are draped over my neck…"
Eyes do show up in this poem, but for tears: "my eyes flow with tears." (verse 16). The yoke isn't there. The poem says the transgressions "…are draped over my neck…"
That's the opposite of what the poem says, friend. It says, "The Lord has rejected all the mighty men in my midst…" Rejected, not honored. So this one is False.
False. The poem says, "The Lord has rejected all the mighty men in my midst…" It goes on to say He "…has summoned an army against me to crush my young warriors." The mighty men aren't being honored.

His neighbors become his foes. The poem says, "The LORD has decreed against Jacob that his neighbors become his foes." Jacob here means his people. The people living right next door turned into enemies.
Empty fields aren't in this verse, friend. The poem says, "The LORD has decreed against Jacob that his neighbors become his foes." The decree is about the neighbors.
No wells in this verse. What the LORD has decreed is that Jacob's "…neighbors become his foes." It's about who lives next door, not what's in the ground.
Righteous. The poem says, "The LORD is righteous, yet I rebelled against His command." Look at what the speaker does here. The speaker doesn't blame anyone else and says the LORD is righteous.
Distant isn't what the poem says about Him. The line is, "The LORD is righteous, yet I rebelled against His command." The speaker calls the LORD righteous and then owns the rebelling.
Silent doesn't show up in this verse, friend. The poem says, "The LORD is righteous, yet I rebelled against His command." Righteous is the word, and the speaker takes the blame for the rebelling.

The young men and maidens. The poem says, "My young men and maidens have gone into captivity." These are the young ones, and the poem asks everyone to look at that suffering. I think it's one of the hardest lines in the chapter.
Judges and scribes aren't named in this verse. The poem says, "My young men and maidens have gone into captivity." Different people, and a different kind of loss.
Singers and gatekeepers aren't in this poem, friend. The captives named here are the "…young men and maidens…" The verse says, "My young men and maidens have gone into captivity."
The speaker's distress. The poem says, "See, O LORD, how distressed I am!" The speaker doesn't dress it up and just asks to be seen. I think that's honest prayer, friend.
The speaker doesn't point to faithfulness at all. The poem says, "…for I have been most rebellious." What gets shown to the LORD is distress: "See, O LORD, how distressed I am!"
Strong walls aren't on the list, friend. The poem asks, "See, O LORD, how distressed I am!" The speaker wants Him to see distress, and it says "my heart is pounding within me…"
True. The poem says of the enemies, "they are glad that You have caused it." They heard about the trouble and they're glad. That's a lonely thing to read, even in a poem.
It's true, friend. The poem says, "All my enemies have heard of my trouble; they are glad that You have caused it." The enemies are glad about the trouble.

explanations.answer: To end up the same way
explanations.explanation: To end up the same way. The poem asks the LORD to bring the day He has announced "…so that they may become like me." Then verse 22 asks Him to "…deal with them as You have dealt with me…" That's the speaker's plea, and the poem doesn't hide how raw it is.
Forgiveness isn't what the speaker asks for here. The poem says, "…deal with them as You have dealt with me because of all my transgressions." The request is for them to end up like the speaker.
Servants don't show up in this request, friend. The poem asks for the day so "…that they may become like me." The speaker wants the enemies to end up where the speaker is.
